links.why: Brushing washes away the sticky film of germs on your teeth before it can make holes.
The tiny germs in your mouth love sugar, and brushing takes them off your teeth.
Your teeth are parts of your body that you can see, and each kind of tooth has its own job.
Two minutes is 120 seconds, so watch the clock while you brush.
Tell someone why we brush twice a day, in your own words.
Soap pulls the oily dirt and germs off your skin so the water can rinse them away.
Washing your body takes away germs and sweat before they make you itchy or sick.
A warm bath or a cool one changes your body heat, and your body works to keep itself steady.
Soap mixes into the water, and the dirty water carries the dirt away.
A bucket bath uses much less water than a long shower, so it saves water.
Soap lifts germs off your hands, and the water rinses them down the drain.
Germs travel on hands, so washing before eating stops them reaching your mouth.
When germs do get in, your body fights them, but clean hands give it less to fight.
Count 20 seconds while you scrub, about as long as singing a short song twice.
While you sleep your muscles rest and your body gets ready for the next day.
You sleep when your side of the Earth has turned away from the Sun and it is dark.
Plants and birds also keep time by the light, just like you do.
If you go to bed at 9 and wake up at 6, you can count how many hours you slept.
Being short of sleep can make people cranky, because feelings and sleep are linked.

acts.name: Falling sick with fever or cold

links.why: When you have a fever, your body is fighting a germ, and it is working hard.
Coughs and sneezes send out tiny drops with germs, so cover your mouth and nose.
Your body is normally steady near 37 degrees, and a fever means it has gone higher.
A thermometer works because the liquid inside takes more room as it gets warmer.
Tell the doctor or your parent clearly where it hurts and since when.

acts.name: Visit to the doctor or clinic

links.why: The doctor looks at your eyes, throat and ears, which tell about your health.
The stethoscope lets the doctor hear your heartbeat and your breath.
Your belly and chest hold organs, and the doctor feels them gently to check each one.
The doctor measures how tall you are and writes the number down.
A doctor, a nurse and a pharmacist each have a different job in keeping people well.
A vaccine teaches your body to recognise a germ, so it can fight it fast if the real germ comes.
Some illnesses spread from person to person, and vaccines help stop them spreading.
Your blood has special cells that fight germs, and they remember what they have met.
Your vaccine card has dates, so you can count how many months until the next one is due.
Health workers keep a record of every child, so the whole community stays safe.
Milk teeth fall out as you grow, and bigger teeth come up to take their place.
Different teeth have different jobs: the front ones cut, and the back ones grind food.
Count your teeth, then count how many are still to come.
The calcium in milk and curd helps make teeth strong.
Ask friends how many teeth each has lost and draw a chart.
Your body changes as you grow from a baby to a child to an adult.
Stand against a wall, mark your height and measure the mark with a tape.
Protein in dal, eggs and milk helps your body build itself as it grows.
Find how many centimetres you grew by taking last year's height away from this year's.
Mark your height each year on a chart and watch the line go up.
Your body fights germs that enter a cut, and a scab forms to cover it.
Washing a cut with clean water and covering it keeps germs out.
Blood travels all around your body, and when you get a cut it thickens to stop the flow.
Pain is a sense too: it tells your body something is wrong.
Your skin is made of tiny cells, and new ones grow to fill the cut.
Muscles get tired when you use them hard, and rest helps them grow strong.
Feel your heart beat faster when you jump, because your muscles need more oxygen.
Bending and stretching use the joints and muscles of your body.
Count your jumps or stretches in tens as you go.
Time yourself to see how long you can hold a pose.
After you run, your heart beats fast and you breathe hard so your muscles get oxygen.
Your muscles ache after a hard run because they were working a lot and need rest.
A stopwatch tells you how many seconds you took to run across the ground.
You can measure the track in metres to see how far you ran.
You feel hot and sweat when you run, and sweating helps your body cool down.
You hold your breath when your head is under water, and breathe in when you come up.
Swimming uses nearly all of your muscles, so it feels tiring afterwards.
Even with your eyes shut, you can feel where your arms and legs are in the water.
Showering after swimming washes off the pool water and what it carried.
Count how many seconds you can hold your breath, or how long a lap takes.
Count out the rupees you give and check the right coins and notes come back.
Add up the price of each thing, then take it away from what you gave to find the change.
A shop buys things from others and sells them to us for a little more.
The shopkeeper, the farmer and the driver all do jobs so the thing reaches you.
Ask politely for what you want and say thank you.
Try asking in Hindi at the shop: "yeh kitne ka hai?"
Count your coins and notes to see how much you have saved.
Each week, add what you saved to what you had before.
Draw a bar chart of how much you saved each week.
Banks keep people's savings safely and often add a little extra for keeping it there.
If a toy costs 200 rupees and you save 20 a week, how many weeks will it take?
There are coins and notes of different values, and you can make the same amount in different ways.
Count up from the price to the amount you gave to find the change.
Money uses place value: a 10 rupee note is ten ones, and a 100 rupee note is ten tens.
Three 5 rupee coins make 15, which is 3 times 5.
Guess whether 100 rupees will be enough before the bill comes.
The short hand shows the hour, and the long hand shows the minutes.
People first made clocks by watching the Sun's shadow move across the ground.
A day is how long the Earth takes to turn round once, and a clock splits it into 24 hours.
Find how long until lunch by taking the time now away from lunch time.
Count by fives round the clock face to get the minutes.
There are 7 days in a week and 12 months in a year, and you can count the days in each month.
People made calendars by watching the Moon and the Sun.
Many Indian festival dates follow the Moon, which is why they fall on different days each year.
Find the date of the next festival and count how many days are left.
The days of the week come in a repeating pattern, again and again.
A letter has a greeting, a message and a sign-off, in that order.
You can write the same letter in Hindi or in your own language to a grandparent.
Start each sentence with a capital letter and end it with a full stop.
The postman carries your letter, and sorters and drivers help it travel.
The address tells exactly where in the town the letter must go.

acts.name: Talking to a shopkeeper or neighbour

links.why: Speak clearly and politely, and wait for the other person to finish before you talk.
Use respectful words such as "aap" when you talk to older people.
A neighbourhood is a community where people help each other.
Each person you meet in the lane or market does a job that helps others.
Ask for the price, and then work out how much to pay.
Your voice makes the air shake, and the phone turns that shaking into a signal.
Your ears pick up the sound that the phone speaker makes.
On a call you cannot always see faces, so say clearly who you are and listen carefully.
Calling grandparents or cousins far away keeps a family close.
Check what time it is where your cousin lives, which may be different from here.

acts.name: Making rotis or cooking with family

links.why: The flat pan gets hot, and the roti cooks and puffs as it heats up.
Wheat grows in a field, is ground into atta, and ends up as your roti.
Dough is soft and can be shaped, but a cooked roti is firmer.
Cut a roti in halves or quarters and share it out.
Measure the water and atta in cups to get dough that is just right.
Wheat gives you energy, and eating it with dal adds protein.
A thali with dal, rice, vegetables and curd gives your body many kinds of food.
Different foods give you different things: energy, protein, or help to stay healthy.
Trace your meal back to the plants, the farmer and the Sun that grew it.
Food that sits out too long can spoil, so keep it covered and eat it soon.
Wash your hands before you eat so germs do not go into your food.
Your body needs water to stay steady, and you lose water when you sweat.
Water comes from rivers, wells or taps, and it must be clean to be safe to drink.
Boiling water kills the germs that can make you ill.
Pour out only the water you need, and use the rest again.
A glass holds about 200 millilitres, so count how many glasses fill a litre.
Hair grows from your skin and helps protect your head.
Oil is thick and slow, and water is runny, so they pour differently.
Washing hair removes the dust and sweat that gather on it each day.
A plait is a pattern of over and under, repeating each time.
Measure how long your hair has grown in a month.
Dirt and germs hide under long nails, so cutting them keeps your hands clean.
Nails protect the tips of your fingers, and they grow slowly all the time.
Nails grow only a few millimetres in a month, so you can measure it.
Germs can get into your mouth if you bite dirty nails.
Cotton clothes soak up sweat in summer, and wool traps warmth in winter.
Wet clothes dry because the water in them turns into vapour in the air.
Your clothes help your body stay warm or cool, depending on what you wear.
Detergent mixes into the water and helps lift dirt out of the cloth.
Cotton clothes come from a plant grown in fields.
The Sun's light warms the Earth, but its rays can burn skin if you stay out too long.
When you get hot, you sweat, and the water on your skin helps you cool down.
Playing is exercise, and your muscles get stronger when you play.
Your shadow gets long in the evening and short at noon because the Sun is at a different height.
Playing with friends makes most people feel happy.
Your body shows feelings: your heart beats faster when you are scared.
You can read how a friend feels by looking at their face and listening to their voice.
Say how you feel in words, and listen when others tell you.
Pick words for feelings that are exact: annoyed, nervous, lonely or proud.
Talk to someone you trust when a feeling is too big to hold alone.
We see when light bounces off things and goes into our eyes.
A glass lens bends light, which is how glasses help your eyes focus.
Your eyes are delicate, so we protect them from dust and from strong light.
A convex lens is thicker in the middle, and a concave one is thinner in the middle.
Very loud sounds can hurt your ears, so keep the volume low.
Every sound starts with something that is shaking.
Sound travels through the air as a wave to reach your ears.
Never put sharp things into your ears.

acts.name: Getting ready for school or class

links.why: Plan your morning with the clock: when to wake, bathe and leave.
Many animals wake with the light, and so do we.
Work out which jobs to do first so you leave on time.
Morning is when your part of the Earth turns toward the Sun.
A routine repeats the same steps every day, like a pattern.
Look both ways, use the crossing, and follow the signal.
Buses, autos, cycles and cars all share the road in different ways.
A moving vehicle cannot stop at once, so stay back from the road.
Bright and reflective colours help drivers see you in dim light.
Say whether you will turn left or right to reach your side of the road.
Trains, buses and autos carry many people over long distances.
When the bus brakes, you lean forward because your body wants to keep moving.
Read the train timetable to find when it leaves and when it arrives.
Follow the route on a map and name the places you pass.
Work out the ticket cost for the whole family.
When you stop pedalling the cycle keeps rolling, because moving things keep moving.
The pedals, chain and wheels let a small push from your legs turn the wheel.
Cycling makes your leg muscles stronger and your heart beat faster.
Brakes press on the wheel and friction slows it down.
Wear a helmet and ride away from busy traffic.
Count how many months or days until your next birthday.
Each year your body changes a little as you grow older.
Cut the cake into equal pieces so everyone gets the same share.
If 12 children each get 2 pieces, then 12 times 2 gives the total.
When you blow on a candle, the flame loses its heat and goes out.
People across India celebrate different festivals, each with its own food, dress and songs.
Many festivals follow the Moon, so their dates move from year to year.
A rangoli often has the same pattern on both sides.
Plan a small budget for what you need for the festival.
Ask elders how this festival was celebrated when they were small.
Grandparents show how a body changes in old age, and you can talk about it kindly.
Ask what life was like when they were your age, and write it down.
Draw your family tree to show who is related to whom.
Speak with your grandparents in your home language and learn new words.
Work out how many years older they are than you.

acts.name: First aid and safety at home

links.why: Keep medicines, knives and matches away from small children.
Run cool tap water over a small burn to take away the heat.
Electricity flows only when a circuit is complete, which is why wet hands near sockets are dangerous.
Clean your hands before you touch a wound.
Know the phone number to call for help and say clearly what has happened.
A baby grows from a single cell in the mother's body before it is born.
A baby changes as it grows, learning to sit, crawl and walk.
A family grows when a baby comes and everyone helps care for it.
A baby's first food is mother's milk, which has what a baby needs.
Compare a baby's weight with your own on a scale.

acts.name: Why do I sweat or why is my heart beating

links.why: Sweat dries on your skin and takes heat away, so you cool down.
Put your hand on your chest and feel the heart pump blood around your body.
Your stomach, lungs and heart are organs inside you that each do their own job.
Count your pulse for one minute and write the number down.
Your heart beats faster when your muscles are working hard.
Food goes down to your stomach and intestines, where it is broken up for your body to use.
Food left out can grow germs that give you a tummy ache.
Drink only clean water, especially when you have a stomach upset.
Washing your hands before meals keeps germs away from your food.
A scale shows how heavy you are in kilograms.
Take last year's weight away from this year's to find how much you gained.
A scale measures the pull of gravity on your body, which pushes down on it.
Guess which of two things is heavier before you weigh them.
Record your weight every few months in a chart.
At a fair many sellers gather, and buyers go from stall to stall to compare prices.
Decide how to spend 100 rupees across the things you want.
A giant wheel turns around its centre and lifts people high.
Look for circles, triangles and squares in the rides and stalls.
Fairs often come with festivals and local crafts.

acts.name: Visit to a bank, ATM or UPI payment

links.why: A bank keeps your money safely and writes down how much you have.
People pay with cash, cards or UPI, and each way moves money from one person to another.
Add what you put in and take away what you took out to find the balance.
Cashiers, managers and guards all work in a bank.
Some of the money we pay as tax is used by the government for schools, roads and hospitals.
Rain comes from water that rose up as vapour and then cooled and fell again.
Your body shivers in the cold to make heat, and sweats in the heat to cool itself.
Puddles disappear because the water turns to vapour and goes into the air.
A thermometer shows how hot or cold the day is in degrees.
Record the weather each day for a month and make a chart.

acts.name: Looking at the moon and stars

links.why: The Moon looks different on different nights because we see more or less of its lit side.
The Sun is a star, but the Moon only reflects the Sun's light.
People joined stars into pictures and named them long ago.
Early people watched the sky to know the seasons and the time.
Note down the Moon's shape each night and count the days between full moons.

acts.name: Taking care of a pet or animal

links.why: A pet needs food, water, shelter and care, like all living things.
Dogs smell far better than people, and cats see better in dim light.
Wash your hands after you touch any animal.
A puppy or kitten grows up into an adult, and then it can have young.
Measure how much food a pet needs each day.
A seed needs water and warmth to begin to grow.
Leaves use sunlight, air and water to make food for the plant.
The plant draws water up from the roots through its stem.
Measure the plant each week and see how much it has grown.
Plants grow in soil made from broken rock and dead plants.
Kitchen scraps turn into soil in a compost pit.
Waste dumped in the wrong place makes air, water and land dirty.
Paper, plastic and metal are different materials, and we sort them into groups.
Reusing things means we need to take less from nature.
Count how much waste your home makes in a week and make a chart.

acts.name: Switching on lights, fan and appliances

links.why: The switch closes the circuit, and then electricity can flow and light the bulb.
Electricity can make light, heat, movement and sound.
A battery stores energy that it gives out when you use it.
Switching off lights and fans we do not need saves electricity.
Look at the electricity bill and see what it costs.
